subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF CANADIAN CITIZENS OF ASIAN UGANDAN ORIGIN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the early 1970s thousands of Ugandans of Asian ancestry were expelled from Uganda by Dictator Idi Amin. Many of these people came to Canada and now consider Canada to be their home.
An outstanding question has always been the repossession of property that these people were forced to abandon in Uganda. Kampala has recently announced rules under which such repossession might take place. Apparently, under the proposed rules, ex-Asian Ugandans will have only 90 days to return to Uganda and will then have to remain there for at least five years before being able to dispose of their rightful possessions. For very obvious reasons such a procedure would be unacceptable to people who are now Canadian citizens and wish to remain in Canada. A very similar problem exists with respect to impounded superannuation and insurance funds.
Therefore, the Government of Canada ought to make appropriate representations to the Government of Uganda to ensure fair and timely treatment for Canadian citizens of Asian Ugandan origin.

Madam Speaker, in Quebec, all agricultural organizations that were consulted agreed with the need to revise the Crow rate in order to correct railway transportation problems in the West.
First of all, and this is very important, there is now agreement that the measures to be applied in the West will not affect the supply or price of feed grain in Eastern Canada. The reason is simple. The 1974 feed grain policy, recently extended until August 1983, ensures diversity of supply for Quebec feeders. They can buy their feed grain locally or in Ontario,
the U.S. or Western Canada. The Canadian Wheat Board must supply feed grain if the private market does not, and does so at a price determined by the price for U.S. corn.
On December 4, 1982, on Radio-Canada, a spokesman for the FPU said that the price in Eastern Canada is determined by the world market. People in the West would have to adjust to that level, and implementation of the Gilson report would not affect our prices.

subsubtopic: LIBERAL MEMBERS' REPLY TO STATEMENT BY CONFERENCE OF CATHOLIC BISHOPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, many Members of this House, as well as Canadians from coast to coast, were rather taken aback by the tone and substance of a statement released yesterday by five Liberal backbenchers in response to the recent statement on the economy by the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops.
It is a sad commentary to see the Government so sensitive to thoughtful criticism of its policies that it must send out a hit team, who used their membership in that same church to justify their advancing the Government's criticism of the Bishops' statement. On the other side of the coin, there are many, many Catholics across Canada who welcomed the Bishops' statement and who support both it and their right to make such a statement. It is disappointing, at a time when Canada is crying out for new directions in its economy, that the Government would react so flippantly to the serious proposals of a major force in our society.
As well, there was a rather disturbing element to yesterday's statement. That was the comparisons used by the Hon. Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). To bring into the debate the states of affairs that exist in such extremist regimes as Chile and El Salvador was, I submit, unconscionable. The implied threat that he made by pointing to the assassination of Archbishop Oscar Romero as an example of the results of church involvement in temporal affairs, does a grave disservice to the right of freedom of expression in this country. These five Liberals owe an apology to the Catholic Bishops of Canada, to the Catholics of Canada, and indeed to all Canadians.

subsubtopic: MOHAWK COLLEGE OF HAMILTON-WORK SKILLS PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Mohawk College of Hamilton, a community college, has been a leader and a pioneer in the development of educational systems which involve employers and training of students. One such program is the co-operative education technique whereby technical and business programs are integrated with industry, business and government throughout Canada. This program provides skills and experience for the student, making him or her particularly valuable as a full-time employee.
This system necessitates the co-operation of the employers to provide work experience during the education terms. This system has the merit of providing students with a modified work program on a year-round basis, and takes the pressure off trying to find a job in the summer only.
Since 1978, the Federal Government has provided Mohawk College with seed money to develop such programs, and Mohawk College has received international recognition for the excellence of the work done. However, current economic conditions are such that the employers find it financially difficult to participate in the work study program.
I would therefore like to recommend that the federal and provincial Governments help the youth of this region in preparing themselves for skilled, full-time jobs, by encouraging employers to participate in these work sharing programs, by providing either a direct subsidy or other financial assistance to employers to cover part of the student wages.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF ATLANTIC FISHERIES CROWN CORPORATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today we discovered that the Liberal Government is again stalling in attempting to solve the problems which are very drastic in the Atlantic fishing industry. Over a year ago the Kirby Task Force was instructed to proceed "on an emergency basis". Today we discovered that the Cabinet is again stalling and dividing itself strictly for political reasons.
The New Democratic Party criticizes and deplores the leaking of the Kirby Report instead of the issuing of that full report to the public of Canada. We call on the Government to act in order to protect the incomes and livelihoods of fishermen in Atlantic Canada.
Today we found out that one Cabinet Minister is calling for one Crown corporation to act in this area. Other Cabinet Ministers want to continue the divide and rule regime which exists at the present time. It is time that the policy of the Government, which protects the fishing corporations in Altantic Canada, stopped. It is time that the Government acted. It is time that the Government set up one crown corporation to control marketing and to help increase the income of Atlantic fishermen.

That this House recognizes that an increased commitment to science and technology is fundamental to the establishment of a new industrial base in Canada, to the rejuvenation of existing industries, to the creation of new employment and the maintenance of existing jobs, and to economic recovery, and that this House condemns the Government for its neglect in failing to aggressively develop policies to promote the advancement of science and technology in this country, for its lack of interest in utilizing and increasing Canada's human potential, and for its failure to adopt the spending targets for science and technology that were established by the Progressive Conservative Government in 1979.
Fie said: Madam Speaker, we chose to make use of this Opposition day to bring attention to the urgent and critically important subject of science and technology. Our motion clearly states our concern over the virtual neglect of this key to economic recovery and survival.
I would like to begin by alluding to remarks made recently by the Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston) in various speeches outside the House. I wish he would have been here to hear these remarks.
He will be here later.

Good. I bring these remarks to the attention of the House partly for the record, partly to offer endorsement of them in principle, certainly to offer encouragement, and partly to take issue with the non-application of them to date by this Government. I would like to make it clear to the new Minister that we welcome him and his expressed views, but we also remind him that only the Minister is new; the problem is not. It is long past the rhetoric stage. In fact, it is even long past the action stage. The subject of this debate is vitally important to Canada and much too important to be a partisan issue.
I am pleased that science and technology is now the responsibility of the Minister responsible for economic development because that is where it should be. As our motion today states, science and technology is fundamental to economic development and an integral part of economic recovery. It has been disregarded for a decade and a half while the world passed Canada by. It must not be disregarded any longer.
The Minister has recognized this fact in his speeches. Everyone who talks about science and technology recognizes it. Why, then, is the Government of Canada not adequately carrying out the vitally needed policies and programs that everyone knows are needed?
Let me quote some of the Minister's recent public remarks about this subject. The first quote is:
Our industrial structure will still have a very strong resource bias because that is our area of strongest comparative advantage.
We agree. But why, then, do the two principal levels of Government tax mining on a wind fall basis so that profits are taxed at a level as high as 60 per cent? Why does the Government plan to introduce a northern development tax which will add to the costs of the mining companies in offsetting the former so-called perks of their employees? This will serve only to drive up the cost of Canada's resources in world markets. Why does the Government's regulatory pricing of petroleum resources serve to reduce, not expand, the exploration and development processes which depend on petroleum fuels and petroleum feedstocks? The petroleum industry in eastern Canada alone, an industry which employees over 100,000 people both indirectly and directly and generates product worth $4 billion annually, has been crippled. It faces imminent collapse within months as a result of destructive tax policies on resources, particularly for feedstocks.
I would like to hear the Minister give a detailed explanation of how he will change the Government's tax policy to revitalize the threatened industry and to protect these 100,000 jobs. Will the Minister back up his own statement and show Canadians that he will do more than his predecessor, more than just



February 4, 1983

mouth technological platitudes, and in fact get our resource sector moving productively, technologically, innovatively and profitably. As a tax lawyer, and even as an author on the subject of taxation, will he undertake to make these badly needed changes at once?
Here is another quotation from the Minister:
It is in the new technology-intensive goods and services that the new jobs will be created. But more crucial, it is in these technology-intensive sectors, and I believe in these sectors alone-
That is a remarkable statement:
-that new challenging and high paying jobs can be created.
Let us contrast that statement of hope and intention with the reality of the fact that in 1980 Canada suffered a trade deficit of $1 billion in computers and related products and, according to the Science Council of Canada, that deficit will rise to $5 billion by 1985. Although the Minister can point to some clearly successful examples of high-tech development, it should be apparent that only a dramatic drive to encourage major advances in these technology-intensive sectors by means of tax incentives and grants will any significant degree of success be reached.
But what has the Government actually done? The Mac-Eachen budget cut the capital cost allowance on the first year after acquisition of the necessary new machinery and equipment of all kinds which is needed to speed up both the research operation and the more efficient production of manufactured goods.
Again, can the Minister explain the difference between the wonderful words he has given to the public and the woeful and destructive actions taken by his colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde)? Even worse, we find that the Department of Finance is now dictating research and development policies. That calls into question the very definition of R and D, the activities in private companies which, up until now, have normally qualified as research. It is even imposing moratoriums on new rulings on the special research investment contracts, the SRICs.
How does the Minister plan to eliminate this stifling bureaucratic impediment to the new technology development which he so rightly describes as being crucial to new job creation in Canada? Even the vice-president of that highly respected corporation, Mitel, complains that "doors have closed" on the SRIC contracts. He says that "favourable rulings stopped in May of 1982, but we are working with the Government to try to open the doors again".
Other people describe the situation in terms of Revenue Canada tightening the screws. Is Revenue Canada to set the control, to control research policy, and pass judgment on the legitimacy of research being carried out, just as it does with regard to Canadian taxpayers who are considered to be guilty until proven innoncent? Or will the Minister point out to Revenue Canada that there is vastly more to be gained through research and the new products and processes it creates
Supply
than the paltry sums to be saved by tightening the screws on research tax options? Why, research pays off at the rate of about 100 per cent a year to Government and, in addition, creates jobs at the rate of 800,000 for every 1 per cent of Gross National Product invested.
Another example of stifling of research in Canada is found in the pharmaceutical industry. Unless the amendments to the Patent Act are repealed, more and more research jobs will be lost to Canada because companies are not afforded the normal patent protection, and all this because of a bureaucratic fiat, a control of research in the country's economy.
Would the Minister undertake to convince the Government that it has been too involved in force-feeding its own bureaucratic growth and control to the detriment of productivity and research? Let me remind the Minister of another of his recent statements. He said:
The difference lies in skills, and that is why education and training and the encouragement of creativity, innovation and enterprise are so important to our future success. Our awareness of the challenges and opportunities that lie ahead must begin in the school system.
How can any reasonable person accept such a clear statement of priority by the Minister in light of the crippling cutback in post-secondary funding which will guarantee even fewer scientists, researchers and technicians in the future than even the deficient numbers being turned out today?
The last quotation of the Minister is a remarkable one. He stated:
I can best describe the urgency and importance of all this by forecasting for you how Canada would fare if we could not manage technological change effectively. Our industrial base, especially manufacturing, would be severely eroded. Unemployment would continue to be high, in the double digits. Our net revenues from resource industry would be severely reduced as our costs rose. The vast majority of the labour force would be forced toward low-paying service jobs.
Has the Minister been away on a long trip, or am I in some kind of a time warp? What is all of this would-be nonsense? These are exactly the problems we are facing today because we have not managed technological change effectively. The Government has totally ignored its obligations to the Canadian people by failing to keep Canadian investment and research at a level equal to the standard of the top technological nations of the world. Back in 1968, Canada expended 1.4 per cent of its Gross National Product on research. The Liberal Government let that figure erode to less than 1 per cent by 1980. When the world was going up, Canada was going down. Last year we invested 1.2 per cent of our GNP on research, on the road back to 1.5 percent by 1985, which is the Government's new, or I should say old, renewed goal. Even if we get there, it will be far too little; but then we would rather let Revenue Canada run our science and technology policies than our scientists and businessmen.
The Minister warns us that in the technology-intensive sectors alone will new challenging and high paying jobs be created. We hope, then, that the Minister will consider the following fact when he thinks of the $5 billion deficit Canada will be facing with regard to computer-related products. France alone will be investing $27 billion over the next five

February 4, 1983
Supply
years in computers and consumer electronic products. This is more money than Canada will spend on all its research, even if it meets its objective of 1.5 per cent of GNP.
I wish the Minister of State for Science and Technology well. I envy him, too. He has inherited a very difficult, but not impossible, task. He will have to educate and convince the dinosaurs in the Liberal Cabinet that Canada is in the age of the information revolution, that eight working Canadians will be producing information in one form or another for every one Canadian who is producing industrial products, and that the information explosion will be a deadly explosion for Canada if we do not gear ourselves up to managing and developing our technology quickly.
I envy the Minister because he has the power to make the changes necessary to bring Canada into the information age, to get the message through to Canadians that the industrial revolution is over, that work, living and education standards are changing and that we must change with them, and that the Government will lead that change, not follow further and further behind. The micro-technologies and bio-technologies are reshaping and will continue to reshape all our standards and values. Our Government has an obligation to lead Canada into the future, not to anchor it into the past.
I believe that the Minister of State for Economic Development is both a competent Minister and a man of his word. He has said that he will soon be bringing forward policies which will launch the initiatives which he believes we need for economic recovery and investment. We applaud that, and we challenge the Minister to make good on these crucial promises.
The Progressive Conservative Party believes that a policy for research and technological and industrial development must embody the specific components of which I will speak. It serves no useful purpose to simply criticize, and so we will offer the Minister a base plan. A national objective, supported by tax and investment policy, should be set to match and eventually surpass those declared goals of competitive, advanced nations and should be constantly monitored for return on investment in both jobs and dollars. Other nations are expending as much as 2 per cent to 3 per cent of their Gross National Product. We should certainly be attempting to match or better that.
An industrial policy must concentrate on the strength of Canada, both human and fiscal. Canada's research and industrial development should be mainly directed to resource-based activities, as the Minister says, and to those opportunities presented by the exigencies of Canada's geography, climate, size or any other particular requirements.
Policy should aim at the broadest application of human skills and the providing of the maximum in personal accomplishment, social opportunity and national wealth generation for the benefit of all Canadians. Policy should emphasize the greater role and responsibilities of the private sector to conduct the larger portion of research for reasons of objectivity, efficiency and directness of result.
Policy should clearly identify and deliberately support advance in technologies and industries; for example, electronics, micro-electronics, bio-technology and other types of high technology which are developed. Policies should create a
favourable environment for research spending and venture capital by means of sensible regulatory and tax systems embodying the proper balance of tax incentives, both positive and negative, grants, Government purchasing practices, export incentives and product mandating encouragement.
Policies should be developed in co-operation with provincial Governments and consider regional needs and strengths. Policies should support a strong basic research role through national and academic institutions. We have done well in these fields in the past but we must do more. Policies should encourage and co-ordinate appropriate educational programs to meet foreseeable scientific, technological, industrial and social requirements.
I found it strange that the secretary of MOSST would go around a year ago with beautiful multi-coloured slides proving conclusively that Canada was producing half as many scientists as it needed, but I did not realize then that the Minister of Finance would take care of the problem and cut the need instead of developing a better streaming of future scientists into the system.
Policies should develop a favourable public appreciation and attitude toward technological and industrial accomplishment and advancement. I look forward to the day when Canadians will see themselves as technologists, scientists and contributors to a world which desperately needs our resources and our brain power.
Policies of Government procurement should be closely tied to, and supportive of, industrial goals. I challenge the Minister to incorporate and achieve these goals. The achievement of them will guarantee Canada's pre-eminence as a strong, healthy, prosperous nation, which is the birthright of all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Hudecki) for his very penetrating question. It is a very serious one about which I think we can do something. Young people in schools today are very much more

aware that we have left the industrial age and entered the information generation age. I mentioned in my speech that eight Canadians will be working in information generation for every one person producing goods in the future. This is likely to continue to a much greater degree, thus providing more jobs in the information sector.
Of course, the information sector includes everything from people who are in advertising, accounting, conceptual design, the making of blueprints or doing anything which comes up to but falls short of the actual production of goods. The development of skills for which we are calling is one that will embrace a much greater involvement of more and more people to do the kinds of jobs which will be needed in the future.
1 am not concerned with the argument that if we put robots in an automotive plant it will cost jobs. That is obvious, but it would only cost assembly jobs. We would replace them with other jobs, such as looking after the robots and looking after designs handled through the CAD-CAM processes. We would simply change the nature of the jobs. The question should not be: Will we lose half the jobs in an automotive plant? It should be: Will we save half the jobs in an automotive plant? Not to do this, not to be right at the top in world-class standards in any kind of operation, is to lose all the jobs. We will end up having no people producing no cars because the cars will be much too costly and much too inefficient.
I think the standards have to be recognized because they are there, not because we want to set them up. They are there, and we must be the best in the world so that we may be the most competitive and the world will buy more and more Canadian products, which will provide more and more Canadian jobs.

Mr. Speaker, I am very impressed with the work the Hon. Member has done in the area of science and technology and with the thinking he has put into his role as critic. He has presented us with a very general framework for policies in the area of science and technology, which I think sets some very broad objectives that are laudible and should be acceptable.
In the area of education, which is of critical concern because we are not training the number of people we need in the sciences or in the research fields, could the Hon. Member put some specifics or some flesh around his objectives as to how we should go about dealing with the problems faced by universities, with the structural difficulties in the universities and with their problems in the reallocation of resources and so on? Could he put some flesh around his objectives in an educational policy as to how the federal Government might take action to improve the situation?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my Member for that question. I will not take refuge in the argument that we are not the Government and we should not, therefore, put specifics or flesh on the bones. It is a perfectly fair inter-Party question.
The fact is that we have taken too much of a "hands-off' position with regard to post-secondary education. I sympathize with the Member and the Government for apparently having such little control in the provincial application of educational

funds with regard to these institutions. Simply I would encourage him and the Government to be more direct and much more involved in the specific streaming of more federal money directly to perceived objectives in post-secondary institutions. I do not think we can take refuge in the fact that they are not ours and therefore we cannot do anything.
Mr. Speaker, I have a two-part question. Should I put the first part of it, obtain a short answer, and then put the second part?

Well, here is my question. As I understand what the Hon. Member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist) said, he believes it is basically the private sector which should do research and development. I would like him to confirm that it is basically a private sector thrust. If that is true, how does he square it with some of the questions Members of his Party asked today? I am referring to the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) and the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), who want Government involvement, it seems to me.
Also it seems to me that the Hon. Member was saying that in research and development it is basically a private sector thrust. If the private sector in Canada does the research and development, why should American companies-and basically we have American companies in Canada, or a branch plant economy-do the research and development in Canada? Why should they not act like they have always acted and conduct the research and development in the United States, not in Canada; in other words, doing it with the parent companies, to our loss here in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I did not say that the private sector should do all the research and development to the exclusion of Government. I said they should all have a share. It is quite obvious in the very expensive areas of farm or agricultural research that even the biggest farm in Canada could not afford the kind of research cost which is attendant to that. There is a clear need for Government participation in those kinds of fields.
Where you are getting into the area of general and broad-based research, it is impossible to direct that from a very few institutions. It should be conducted in a way that allows Canadians in every walk of life, in every institution, in every skill to come forward with the kind of research and innovation of which we are capable. This happens every day in every company that has a research department. It is far more efficiently done, far better directed and far more profitable to all of the country. We are talking about the benefit of all the country.
I happen to have been involved in a company which was once American, as the Hon. Member said, and is now Canadian. There was a changeover from the research which came

Mr. Speaker, I too join with the Hon. Member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist) in condemning the record of research and development of the Liberal Government, especially in the last decade, which I
would call the lost decade. That decade saw our expenditures on research and development drop to less than 1 per cent of GNP. It was a shameful decade that saw a major downgrading of our major universities and our research capacity.
The record of the 1970s is the strongest example of the type of neglect and mismanagement that the Trudeau Government has inflicted upon Canadian society. It is a national embarrassment and disgrace. It is a disgrace that we ended up having as much of our Gross National Product being expended on research and development as countries like Ireland, Portugal and Spain. It put us into that class of country. I agree with the Conservative Member that Canada should be, and has the capacity, the ability and the need to be, a first-class country in terms of research and development.
There is much that needs to be done in this country. Our position in many ways is unique, geographically, politically, socially and economically. There is a tremendous need and opportunity for having an innovative society with a strong research and development sector.
It is not a case that we are a small country and that we do not have the population base. I point, for example, to the Nordic countries, Norway, Denmark, Sweden and Finland, which are very much like us in climate, population size and resources, yet their private industry spends almost twice as much on research and development. Their industrial labour force is about 25 per cent larger than ours. Those countries have had coherent plans to ensure adequate research and development being done in their countries. It is not an excuse that can wash when we say that Canada just does not have the population base or market base to allow a healthy research and development sector.
The sad record of the seventies continues, the record of mismanagement. Our universities are in a state of financial uncertainty. They do not know what grand scheme the boys across the way are plotting now. They do not have any assurance that financing of universities will continue on a predictable basis in the years ahead. For the last number of years they have been existing in this area of uncertainty. Is it deliberate Government policy to create this uncertainty or is it just a mindlessness we have seen so often being exhibited by this Government?
As well, there exists a lack of coherent policy in terms of taxes and grants to encourage the private sector to expend money on research and development. There has been no clear, precise statement, strategy or goals presented by the Government that would allow the private sector to have some feeling as to where the Government wants the country to go. There is no formulation of coherent policies and goals. We continue to flounder in uncertainty and insecurity.
We have a new Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Johnston). Like the Conservative speaker, I too welcome him to this most important job. Perhaps in the long run it is the most important of all the Ministries.
February 4, 1983

Like the Conservative Member, 1 too am disappointed in the record so far. We do not see a coherent program emerging that can begin to shed some light and provide some leadership to Canadians, whether in the private sector or in universities, people who are engaged in research and development. There is no coherent policy and no coherent goals coming from the Government.
While in many ways I agree with the Conservative motion, it does miss a few essential points. The essential reason why we have a small amount of research and development in Canada today is that our private sector has not invested the sums of money in research and development as they have in other countries, such as the Nordic countries, Germany, Holland, the United States and Japan.
We must ask the question why. The answers are there, Mr. Speaker. Studies after studies have demonstrated that most of the industries in Canada are branch plant industries. It is not so much the fact they are foreign owned which prohibits the development of R and D in Canada; it is the economic structure which they create in Canada which works against development of R and D. The simple fact is that we as branch plants do not have the opportunity of doing research and development in Canada. It generally gets done in the home country. That is where the scientists and the labs are. That is where research and development work gets done.
Sometimes research can be done in one country, say Germany, and developed somewhere else, say Taiwan, and there is not even a relationship between the research part and the development part. That is the major reason we have low R and D in Canada. In fact the former Minister of State for Science and Technology suggested in a speech to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association a year or so ago that it would require an increase of some $2.4 billion invested in R and D, and most of that will have to come from the private sector if we are to achieve our goal of 1.5 per cent of our Gross National Product going to research and development.
The question then arises, how can we make the private sector, particularly the foreign-owned private sector, make its contributions towards research and development in Canada? I hasten to add it is the foreign sector, not the Canadian privately-owned industries, which are laggards in terms of their expenditures in R and D. In fact, their record is pretty good. It is the foreign-owned companies which make us into a branch plant economy and prevents us from developing our own research and development community here in Canada.
It seems obvious to me that if the Government is to develop a coherent strategy to achieve the 1.5 per cent of our Gross National Product going to R and D, it must first and foremost address itself to the question of how we can get the multinationals to spend a decent amount of their profits in Canada for R and D. We have heard of no solution to that central problem from either our Conservative or Liberal friends. And until we come to a solution to that problem we will always remain a
Supply
second-class country in terms of our scientific research and development.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I hasten to add that it is not the fault of the Canadian people. I believe as a people we are generally well educated. We have some excellent universities. In fact, our past record of major discoveries in the world goes far beyond that expected from our population. For example, oil was first discovered in Petrolia, Ontario, but the oil industry was developed somewhere else. The extraction of kerosene from coal was a process discovered here, but again was developed somewhere else. The telephone was invented here in Canada, but again developed somewhere else.
Perhaps historically the biggest R and D blunder of all time came as a result of a decision taken by a Progressive Conservative Government to scrap the Avro Arrow. This decision, Mr. Speaker, cost the jobs of hundreds and thousands of skilled scientists and engineers, wiping out a technology which the United States gobbled up. We used to refer to Los Angeles as the fourth largest Canadian city because of the large number of engineers and scientists who left Canada to work in the American space program. In fact, our greatest contribution to the American space program was not the "arm" but the scientists and engineers we supplied to the U.S.
But there is a deeper question which we have to address ourselves to as Members of Parliament, and that is a question which does not very often get asked; that is, research and development for whom? To benefit whom? Research and development for what purpose? I would maintain, Mr. Speaker, that just blindly throwing money into research and development is not good enough. I can see that the two old Parties are on the verge of panic as they scramble for a solution to the economic mess which this present system has created. They would have us believe that technology offers the golden way out; but technology at all costs is not necessarily the solution. For example, there are some fundamental problems which will affect Canadians with the unmindful introduction of the new technology. In micro-technology there is the whole question of VDTs and health problems. Unless Government plays a responsible role in the development of this new technology, we will eventually have to pay in terms of increased health costs, and all the health problems this could create for untold thousands of people, particularly women, across the country.
Then there is the question of unemployment with respect to robotics in industry. For example, the GM plant in Lordstown, Ohio brought in robots and displaced some 10,000 workers. Yet did the price of cars go down? No, it did not.
A central question which also has to be asked is, how does throwing people out of work give them the money and opportunity they need as consumers to buy the goods produced? For example, over one-half of the telephone operators, mainly women, lost their jobs at B.C. Tel when it automated its switchboard system. Women are particularly hard hit by the developments in the micro-technological field, because women have always been last hired and first fired. Technology at the expense of people will make such inequalities even worse.

February 4, 1983
Supply
Some say the new technology, the robots, the micro-technology and so on, will create as many jobs as will be displaced. There is no study, Mr. Speaker, of which I am aware, which proves beyond doubt that that indeed will be the case. In fact, I believe it is safe to assume that hundreds of thousands of people can no longer become productive workers, that they will, in essence, become obsolete. What to do with that large section of our population which is going to be displaced is something to which Parliament and Government should address itself.
We come back to the question: Technology for whom? Research and development in whose interests? Our Party, Mr. Speaker, is opposed to just throwing money at the private sector, trying to seduce them with greater and greater grants, hoping that in the end they will do their R and D here. There are many countries in the world trying to do the same. Are we going to try to outbid each other in terms of incentives? If the public, as the public should, makes investment in R and D, we have to make certain that that R and D helps and benefits the Canadian people; but the past record shows that very often this is not the case. I point out, as an example, the mounds of money in tax incentives and direct grants which we have given the oil industry for research and development in the extraction of gasoline and oil from heavy oil, the drilling in the North, new technologies which did not exist before. These new technologies were paid for out of public funds, yet we do not own those technologies. The patents are owned by the few multinational oil companies, and they will use the control of those patents, Mr. Speaker, to blackmail Government and Canadian society into doing their will. For us to spend the money to develop new technologies and discoveries which are then owned by the multi-nationals who ship them out of the country is unacceptable to us.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak on another side of this issue, commonly called "appropriate technologies". These are technologies which do not increase the concentration of wealth and power into fewer and fewer hands, or technologies which allow for greater central control over more and more people's lives.
However, there is the possibility of developing technologies which allow greater independence and greater self-sufficiency. A prime example of that is energy. If we spend the money needed to build a nuclear plant instead on home insulation and conservation, the energy saved will exceed the energy produced by that nuclear plant. At the same time, developing nuclear technology will mean greater central control over people's lives. Developing conservation technologies, Mr. Speaker, allows greater freedom for people because there is less dependence on utility companies and banking and high finance interests. It gives people a greater degree of freedom. To develop appropriate technologies, Government has to play a central role.
Since being elected to this House I have been concerned about the whole question of herbicides and pesticides. I see
tremendous problems in terms of spoiling our water and land. Yet it is the technology of herbicides and pesticides which is now very often forcing farmers into bankruptcy because of their high cost. They are dependent on that technology to control weeds and inspects, even though it has been shown a lot of insects are now developing resistance to these chemicals. And these technologies were developed because of the profit motive. However, a new technology of biological control and different and better farming methods can be developed. That does not mean anyone is going to make a profit on it other than the farmer, but it does mean greater independence for the farmer.
As we move into the twenty-first century, Mr. Speaker, major technological and social changes will occur. We need a Government with a notion as to where we want to go as a society, to develop not only an economic strategy but also a social strategy. We cannot have a research and development strategy without an economic and social strategy; they are all one. We must begin to define the goals of our society. That means input from universities and the scientific community, labour and business, fishermen and farmers, and retired people. We need a coherent policy, a coherent plan. We do not have that now. Therefore, we are in support of the motion introduced by the Conservative Party today.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as you know, I spent some considerable time on the special task force on energy, and if there was anything we learned it was about where we are going to be looking for the main source of energy in the long term. The answer we received from the best laboratories and universities in the world dealing with this subject is that the only hope for mankind to have an abundant source of energy in the future was fusion. I would like to have the position of the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) as to whether or not he would accept that.

Mr. Speaker, I am naturally hesitant about any industry or technology which requires such tremendous capital investment. Given the reality of energy today as opposed to a year ago or even six months ago, we are finding that energy projects require heavy capital investment. Indeed, they are the dinosaurs of the industry. I understood that the committee as well recommended that the path to the future was through hydrogen, the most abundant element in the world today. It is my hope and expectation that R and D will go into solar power, and from there into hydrogen.
The Chairman of the National Research Council suggested to me in committee a year or so ago that he felt that within five to ten years electricity from the sun will be as cost-competitive as that from all other sources. If that is so, if we can get electricity from the sun and at the same time develop hydrogen power to run our cars, trucks and tractors, then 1 suggest we have something which is environmentally sound and does not require massive capital investment. It will allow every country, almost every community, particularly in the Third World, to attain energy self-sufficiency without going into debt up to their necks. They would have a bountiful
February 4, 1983

supply of energy to light their lamps and run their tractors. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that for me that is the path we should be following.

Mr. Speaker, I have three short questions in response to that answer. When you speak about the sun, in fact what you are talking about is fusion. If you want to supply electrical needs through the power of the sun, then you are talking about technology which in fact is both capital-intensive and has as many inherent dangers as a local nuclear plant.
My first question is whether the Member would support the ideas put forward by the Hon. Member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist) in his opening statement dealing with one-product mandating, whether it is a foreign or Canadian company. Then there is adjustment of the tax system to provide incentives for high-risk research and development. That is the short question.

Mr. Speaker, the notion of product mandating I think has a lot going for it. I would include in there that we develop those technologies appropriate for Canada, those which meet our real needs as a country. Energy, transportation and communications are areas which naturally fall into that category. The problem is getting agreement. Studies have shown that by the very nature of multinational corporations and our branch plant economy, very often research and development done in Canada has no relationship to our real needs as a country.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising in debate. I am rising today as Minister of State for Science and Technology more than in my capacity as Minister of State for Economic Development.
I would like to say that it is significant, as has been pointed out by one of the speakers who preceded me, that these two ministries come under the responsibility of the same Minister because of the importance of science and technology to economic development in this country. That necessity has been recognized now in many other countries in the western world, and I suggest that in itself is some indication of the importance which this Government attaches to science and technology.
At the outset I would like to say how much I enjoyed the speeches made by the Hon. Member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist) and by the Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong). While it is true that I take issue with a number of the partisan points which they attempted to score in the course of debate, I suppose that is to be expected.
Unlike yourself; you never score partisan points.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
At the same time I felt there were some very constructive suggestions put forward upon which I will be commenting during the course of my intervention.

I may also add, Mr. Speaker, that I am most impressed with this procedure which enables Hon. Members to exchange views. Unfortunately, the Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong) did not remain in the House to answer questions that might be forthcoming. This creates some problems for Hon. Members who would like to ask some questions about the speech he just made in the House.

Apart from that weakness in today's proceedings which I doubt will arise very often, I do think this is really a very constructive kind of procedure, particularly in terms of a
subject like science and technology in which all Members of this House are so passionately interested in today's world.
I felt 1 should begin by looking carefully at the motion proposed by the Hon. Member for Scarborough East and providing some analysis of it in terms of the Government's policy in the past, in the present and in the future. The motion reads:
That this House recognizes that an increased commitment to science and technology is fundamental to the establishment of a new industrial base in Canada-
That is the first point made by the motion and I would like to speak to that just for a moment. I am not clear and 1 hope I will have the opportunity to ask, although I do not see the Hon. Member for Scarborough East in the House, what was specifically intended by "a new industrial base", in light of the comments that followed during the course of his intervention.
You may recall, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Member spoke of Canada having a very important resource base, a very important strength in that sector, that in all likelihood it would continue to be one of our strengths and that it must be built upon. Obviously, technology has a very significant role to play in enabling Canada to maintain and expand upon its competitive position in that sector.
I am not sure what the Hon. Member means by new industrial base. I suggest that we have a very strong, well established industrial base in Canada and upon that base we must build further. Technology, of course, is the key for us to build further in that sector.
We hear much of Canada being by-passed by other countries and about our lack of commitment and effort. In fact, 1 would be the last to say that we do not require a sound, ongoing technology policy. I would be the last to say that there is not more to be done. But I would also be the last to say that we have not accomplished a great deal and that we do not have a record of achievement of which we must be very proud.
Too often it seems to me that one reads in the press and in reports by economists about Canada's falling rate of productivity. When I say "too often", I am not suggesting that we should not all be conscious of that rather lamentable performance in productivity, particularly during the 1970s.
Canadians, by and large, do not realize that Canada is still one of the most productive countries in the world. In the OECD report on historical statistics for the period 1960 to 1980, the real gross domestic product per employed persons of selected countries is compared with that of the United States which, incidentally, and notwithstanding its lamentable performance in improving productivity, remains the most productive country per worker among the countries cited. The countries are the United States, Canada, France, West Germany, Japan and the U.K.
I am not sure that Members of this House realize that Canada is still ranked second among those countries in terms of real productivity; that is, real gross domestic product per employed person. But what is also true is that we have been

February 4, 1983

rapidly slipping in terms of improving our rate of productivity. In that category Canada is a dismal second to last among those countries. In fact, I am sorry to say that between the period 1973 to 1980 Canada is ranked last among those countries with effectively no productivity increase over the period. That is the problem we must address.
It is important for us to realize that we begin from a very sound base achieved over many years of sound policies, of research and development and of innovation in the industries of this country which have brought us the standard of living which all Canadians enjoy. We have many winners in this country; let us not forget that. Many of them have been due to the programs which have contributed to create that industrial base. I would like to cite a number of programs which this Government has introduced over the years. If there are any questions flowing from them, I would be more than pleased to respond.
The programs which are the best known and which have played major, key roles, I suggest, in terms of keeping Canadian industry competitive and also at the leading edge of technology in so many fields, include the Enterprise Development Program and the Defence Industry Productivity program, both of which are programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce.
A more recent program, Support for Technology Enhanced Productivity Program, is another program of the Department of Industry. Then we have the Unsolicited Proposals Program in the Department of Supply and Services. I see my colleague the Minister for Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) is here today. He is responsible for the administration of that Program to which I have just referred as well as the Source Development Fund, another creative program. This program will have a major impact upon the technology of Canadian firms, also introduced at the instigation of our current Minister of Supply and Services during the current term of this Government. In addition, there are several important programs in the National Research Council of Canada.
I would be remiss in not paying tribute to the work of the National Research Council and the extraordinarily enviable international reputation that it enjoys. It is another institution of which we can be justifiably proud. There we find the Industrial Research Assistance Program as well as Programs for Industry Laboratory Projects.
Each of these programs plays a very significant role in having contributed, and continuing to contribute, to that very important industrial base which Canadians enjoy in this country. I might also mention in passing, because I know that some Members in the House were present, that our colleague the Minister of Supply and Services, who is in the House today, hosted just a few short days ago a celebration of the tenth anniversary of the Science Centre of the Department of Supply and Services. There was a magnificent display of the products and advanced technology that have been produced
Supply
through a number of these programs operating under the umbrella of the federal Government.
I suggest that when we talk about science policies and technology policies, let us never lose sight of the fact that we in Canada are not in the technological backwaters of the world. In fact, we have much technology to export. Of course, we still have great potential ahead of us and it is to realize that potential ahead of us in this world of rapidly changing technology that our efforts must be directed. That is the direction in which we are moving.
I mentioned a moment ago that we must not forget our winners. I thought I would perhaps this afternoon cite some of the lesser known winners in Canada, most of whom have enjoyed the support of these programs. I expect that most Members of the House are familiar with the achievements of companies like Northern Telecom and Mitel in the international arena, and CAE Industries, particularly in the area of aircraft simulators where it has no peer in the international arena.
There are many other companies in this country which are much lesser known. Just a few months ago, when I was speaking in Toronto, I thought I would look up some of these companies to see how many small threshold firms and others have carved out a niche for themselves in the international arena. Canadians are probably not aware of many of these companies. For example, the Industrial Research Assistance Program which I referred to earlier had contributed some $2 million to Abco, which is a Lunenburg, Nova Scotia plastics and equipment manufacturing company. The sales of that company, which is situated in Lunenburg, have risen from $5 million in 1972 to $30 million in 1981. The number of employees has climbed to over 400 from a base of 150 at the beginning of that period. New products that this company has developed through R and D have permitted it to make as much as 80 per cent of its sales on international markets.
I could go through a number of companies that have had similar successes. For example, there is the International Submarine Engineering Company of Port Moody, British Columbia. I have already referred to Mitel. There is such a number of them that time does not really permit me to cite them all. I can cite them from every area of the country, whether it is Intera Environmental Consultants of Calgary or SED Systems of Saskatoon which is a very well known company to Canadians, certainly in that area.
I should perhaps refer to one program which I believe was directly a result of some of the programs of the Department of Supply and Services which I referred to earlier. It is the Services Converto-Braille-Cypitot-Galarneau of Hull, Quebec, which has permitted the development of a computer terminal that gives the blind access to information services such as Telidon, which is another great Canadian technological achievement, the Canadian Press News Services, libraries and so on.
We have much world-class technology in Canada. We are starting from a very sound base. When we look at this motion, which I do not have a great deal of quarrel with apart from the

February 4, 1983
Supply
conclusion, I think we should bear in mind that we are moving forward from an enviable position and have not allowed Canada to stay in the backwaters of technology and innovation as so many observers have often suggested.
Reference is made in the second part of the motion to a policy which supports the rejuvenation of existing industries. We all know that many countries in the western industrialized world today are faced with the phenomenon of the so-called sunset industries. Hopefully, some of these industries can be moved from the sunset back to the sunrise through the application of new technologies. This Government is attempting to do this.
I expect that most Members of the House are familiar with the very substantial financial commitment that this Government has made to that very issue of rejuvenation of existing industries in order to bring them back into a competitive position. I need only mention such programs as ILAP or C1RB, which is directly concerned with the so-called soft sectors-

-or the "secteurs mous", as they say in Quebec, namely, textiles and footwear. It is therefore very important to realize that we have made a real effort in those areas. If I remember correctly, we spent $267 million on this program, which is aimed at improving and updating companies in these sectors and also at assisting employees who will be affected by the conditions in the sectors in question.

It is exactly in the spirit of this motion that the Government has in fact moved. As I have said, there is $267 million in that program alone, not to mention an additional $400 million, as I recall, in the ILAP Program to provide industrial adjustment assistance both to industries and, of course, to the employees themselves, who are affected because emerging technologies in other countries and lower labour rates have had a dramatic impact on their ability to compete in international markets.
The motion also refers to the creation of new employment and the maintenance of existing jobs. There is no doubt in anyone's mind that the new technologies and the modernization of plants will have an impact on the job market. Therefore, there is perhaps a certain amount of paradox in the motion when we are being told, on the one hand, that we should introduce new technologies but should maintain existing jobs, on the other hand. That does not mean that we cannot create new jobs, but I suggest that the introduction of new technologies, such as robotics in the automobile assembly line which was referred to earlier, are bound to displace assembly line workers. I do not think there is any doubt of that. It is somewhat incompatible to say that we are to maintain existing jobs and improve productivity at the same time by introducing new technology.
By the same token, I would say that Governments, industry and labour working together must come to grips with those jobs that are displaced through retraining programs, and
efforts to bring those people who are affected by new technologies to a level of education and "formation" which will enable them to take advantage of the new and exciting opportunities that technology itself brings.
For every robot that one puts on an assembly line, there will be requirements for additional technicians, engineers and programmers who will be responsible for the software that will go into the micro-computers which will operate that robotics system. In fact, many of the jobs that will be displaced will be jobs that will be unattractive. They will be arduous jobs that will be replaced by more stimulating and challenging jobs. The quality of the work environment will, in turn, improve. But at the same time, there is that transitional period through which we as Governments must pass; and I say as "governments" because much of this responsibility must be shared with provincial Governments as well as other sectors. We must ensure that the workers of this country are not fearful of that necessary change because we know that they in turn will be protected from the harsh effects of that change and will prosper from the benefits which new technology will bring. However, I say that it would be unrealistic to suggest that new technology will not have an impact on some of these existing employments. In fact, it should have, because we should replace some of those dreary, assembly line and clerical jobs with ones which are more challenging and better paying.
I would now like to turn to the last part of the motion wherein the mover, the Hon. Member for Scarborough East, in the normal way condemns the Government, and the condemnation was understandably supported by the Hon. Member for Regina East. As stated, the motion reads:
-condemns the Government for its neglect in failing to aggressively develop policies to promote the advancement of science and technology in this country, for its lack of interest in utilizing and increasing Canada's human potential, and for its failure to adopt the spending targets for science and technology that were established by the Progressive Conservative Government in 1979.
Allow me to say that, in the few minutes I have been on my feet this afternoon, I believe I have underlined and pointed out a number of programs which have been very successful. When we speak of Government effort, let us consider the record of rhetoric instead. It is all very well to have "targets", but what we on this side of the House look to is performance. I would like to point out to the House that we have steadily moved up our commitment since assuming office in 1980, that we are right on track in achieving 1.5 per cent of GNP and R and D by 1985.
One hundred and fourteen jobs in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: In 1980, it was 1.07 per cent, and in 1982, it was estimated to be 1.2 per cent. I suggest to Hon. Members that in 1985 it will be 1.5 per cent. It is my wish and that of other Hon. Members in the House that that trend continue so that by the year 1990 it will be 2 per cent or even better.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Let me give some more striking examples in terms of annual incremental percentage growth of commitment to the gross expenditure on research and development in various sectors. In 1980 we increased the federal commitment by 15 per cent, in 1981 by 21 per cent, and in 1982 by 17 per cent. More importantly, the incentives which we have provided to the private sector permitted the industrial sector to increase its 1980 percentage by 18 per cent, by 26 per cent in 1981 and by 23 per cent in 1982. The NDP critics have said that industry is not doing its share. Industry is indeed beginning to do its share in a most dramatic way.
While we are on the subject of targets, I was reading a speech by the former Minister of Science and Technology for the Conservative Government, Mr. Grafftey, given back in 1979.
Not a bad target.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext: He was discussing the university sector and told us that the Conservatives would increase funding to NSERC to 32 per cent. He made the announcement that there would be a 32 per cent hike in 1980-81. Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order, please. I would imagine that the House would have no difficulty in extending the courtesy to the Minister of allowing him to speak for a couple of moments in order to complete his remarks. speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I thank Hon. Members of the House for their indulgence. I will finish my remarks very quickly. Because of the importance which we all attach to the matter, I will finish on a very non-partisan note. I made the point concerning NSERC. Those are the facts, and I think an examination of the record will clearly demonstrate the commitment of the Government to R and D. Notwithstanding cutting back in other sectors, the Government and Members of this side have consistently prodded for more and more spending on research and development.
I was very impressed with the intervention of the Hon. Member for Scarborough East, perhaps more by his comments than by his motion, because when he came to the end of his comments, unlike most spokesmen for the Conservative Party he actually put forward a number of concrete suggestions.
They were pretty good too.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
He put forward the kinds of things which a technology policy, in his view, should embrace. He suggested that we should be building on the comparative advantages of this country and he referred to the resource base. We all agree
Supply
with that. He said he wanted to emphasize that the private sector has an important role to play in research and development. Not only do we agree with that, but the numbers to which I have just made reference also show this to be true.
You are a Tory, Don.

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
I would suggest that, notwithstanding the criticism we have heard of the fiscal system, Section 37 of the Income Tax Act has been instrumental in providing incentive to the industries of this country to invest in R and D. In fact, it is one of the most generous provisions of its kind in any western industrialized nation. That is not to say that it could not be modified. That is not to say that it cannot be improved, and it will be improved if it needs to be improved. However, I am saying for the record that it has been very successful in attracting funds into the R and D sector.
The Hon. Member has referred to the necessity of advancing technology and applications of new technology in the industrial sector, what is commonly referred to as "innovation". I agree with that as well. He spoke of a favourable environment being created for research and development and for venture capital. We agree with that. He spoke of the importance of having a co-operative relationship with provincial Governments. I agree with that and would like to encourage provincial Governments to devote more of their resources to R and D. In fact, in each of my meetings with provincial Governments in my role as Minister of State for Regional and Economic Development, the issue of technology has been one of highest priority. I can assure Your Honour that we will be working closely with the Provinces to ensure that we create a synergism so that not only will we be able to spend 1.5 per cent of Gross National Product on R and D by 1985, but also that it is well spent to ensure that the desired results of those targets, which are important, are achieved.
The Hon. Member emphasized the importance of strong basic research through such organizations or institutions as NSERC. We agree with that. He dealt with the awareness issue at some length. Nothing could be more important than making Canadians aware of the opportunities awaiting us as a nation if we embrace these areas of advanced technology. I know that the Hon. Member for Vancouver Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) said the same thing in the House some weeks ago. He was then quite constructive as well. He also spoke of the importance of Government procurement in terms of developing technology.
I realize that I am going on a bit, Mr. Speaker. Let me just say that there is a paper before a number of my colleagues on technology policy, and I can assure Hon. Members of this House that not only will it address all of the issues which have been raised here today, the constructive issues and suggestions, but that it will also go much further in some areas. I look forward, on the basis of today's exchange, to the support of Members in this House from all Parties when these policies are presented.

speechtext: The Chair will recognize the Hon. Member for Northumberland-Miramichi (Mr. Dionne) to ask a question and, following that, other Hon. Members.

I was happy to hear him say that one of the roles of research and development is to maintain employment and to help find alternative employment for those whose jobs are affected by new technology. I want to remind him that in my own constituency, 1,500 jobs are affected by new technology in national defence. Can we count on the full resources of both of his Ministries to help us find alternate employment and job opportunities on the Miramichi so that the peole of Miramichi will be able to lead productive lives?
In his comments, he also referred to the National Research Council. I agree with his laudatory remarks. However, I remind the Minister that New Brunswick is the only Province in Canada which does not have a unit of the National Research Council.
