speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the question of the Hon. Member, the Government is very sensitive, as he knows, to the problems faced by him in the Miramichi area, particularly with respect to the Chatham base. Every effort is being made to find alternatives which will provide employment for the people affected in that area. Through the initiative of the regional Minister, the Member himself and others, the Government has taken initiatives in New Brunswick such as the establishment by Mitel at Buctouche of a facility which is very significant in terms of high technology in the area.
With respect to the NRC, there are projects under consideration. I am not sure I can give an assurance that they should be placed necessarily on the Chatham base, but there is no doubt as technology improves that it should be available to every region of the country by national institutions, and that is our intention.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister. It concerns the policy paper which is now before Cabinet. We have awaited this paper for quite a while. I know that he has taken some time to put it all together and that he is in a new position, but I expected that it might come out before the Christmas break. Can the Minister give us any idea when it will come out? Will it address the serious problems in the forest industry which could be remedied by putting research and development money into that industry?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I see my role as Minister of State for Economic Development and Minister of State for Science and Technology as really trying to establish a framework with my colleagues within which various programs can move forward by line departments. There is no doubt that there is important research and development to be done in the forestry sector. It has to be done. Unfortunately, during a period of recession of the kind we are experiencing, companies in that sector are less inclined to invest in research and development because they are simply trying to meet payrolls and to fund ongoing necessary costs. That point has been made to us. It is not a problem, I might say, that is unique to the forestry sector.
We are indeed moving forward in that area. In fact, the issue of the forestry sector will be addressed in some detail this weekend at a caucus gathering in Thunder Bay. I expect we will have a good exchange of views and some very clear suggestions by Members from the areas affected by the problems in the forestry sector and the lack of research and development in that sector.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister talked glowingly about more stimulating jobs. Is he aware that many women across the country today are working on word processing machines for not very much more money? Even if one wants to go to the washroom, one has to plug in a key. In the old days one had to ask the boss or the foreman; now one has to ask the machine. Does he really think that is progress?
The Minister speaks highly of sunset and sunrise industries, the winners and the losers, like all Atari Liberals do. Is he aware of a recent study from Massachusetts of one area which got into high-tech that showed the salaries for a few people- engineers, programmers and so on-went very high, but that the rest of the people had to go into the service industries with low-paying salaries. Compared with the way society used to be with older-type industries such as steel manufacturing and so on, where people made the same salaries, the community has basically changed.
Is that the kind of Canada he would like to see when he speaks about more stimulating jobs? Does he recognize the kind of danger inherent in the new high-tech industry about which he so flamboyantly and conservatively speaks? Does he see the danger? What steps would he take to prevent the kinds of things which are happening now, as indicated in the first study conducted in Massachusetts?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) is speaking very much with his tongue stuck in his cheek. Not too many weeks ago I heard him speak in the House, and he certainly did not sound like a neo-Luddite, as he seems to today. The inference I would draw from his remarks is that he feels Canada should reject the technological revolution which is reshaping industries all over the world.
I do not think Canada has a choice in joining that revolution, if we intend to maintain the standard of living to which Canadians have not only grown accustomed but to which they
February 4, 1983

are entitled, given the potential of the country both in terms of natural and human resources. It is our job to manage the technological change. It is our job as a Government to take the lead, and be seen to take the lead, in managing that technological change for the benefit of all Canadians and to ensure that the kinds of problems to which the Hon. Member alluded do not take place. Essentially, that is the point I attempted to make during my remarks.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Minister. He has learned his lesson in law school well, that when one has a weak case, assertively state it and volubly state it. He has certainly done that today.
I have two quotations on which I would ask him to comment. The first is from Dr. Larkin Kerwin of the National Research Council wherein he said:
We currently spend less than any industrialized country on new research.
In other words, we are the worst of all. I would also point out to him that by 1985 Japan will be spending 4 per cent on research, compared with the magnificent sum of 1.5 per cent about which he talked for Canada. Most industrialized countries are over 2 per cent right now.
The second quotation is one from Jack Donegani, President of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, wherein he talked about the Liberal Government and said:
-the Government has deliberately allowed Canadian federal laboratories to suffer through a decade of stagnation since the Lamontagne Commission's review of Canadian science policy. During this time, there has been inadequate hiring of newly trained scientists except to replace retirees. Opportunities for Government scientists to keep their training up to date have been inadequate and active participation in scientific conferences, workshops or professional committees requiring occasional travel has been restricted to an absurd degree.
In view of his beautiful words about what the Government is doing, how does the Minister respond to these two quotations?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the accusation is that we should be doing more as a country, I would agree with it. I concur with Dr. Larkin, but if we are to do more, let us do it in a way which reaps the best possible benefits for the country. Let us not throw money at a problem. Let us make sure that the funds which are being spent are expended well and effectively. This means that we should not have duplication and conflict in different regions. This means that we should put our shoulders to the wheel and have a real national effort on research and development. We are moving very quickly in that regard.
By adding vast sums of money before the communities have put in place the necessary infrastructure and laboratories, the necessary engineers and skills at the university level, supported by the Provinces in particular because they have responsibility for university education, we have to move in a way which maximizes the contributions we are making and does not create an enormous amount of waste. In so far as the latest numbers I have for several countries in 1980 are concerned, it is true that we are behind. We were at 1.02 per cent of the GNP. France was at 1.83 per cent, Japan was at 1.95 per cent and the United States was at 2.47 per cent. None of those
Supply
countries in 1980 was at anything like the 3 per cent, if I recall that the Hon. Member suggested.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Minister was talking about 1985. The projections for Japan in 1985 are 4 per cent.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. That is not a point of order. The Hon. Member could have risen on a question or a comment if he wished. 1 urge him to continue during the time available with his comment.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could direct a question to the Minister. The Minister mentioned that there was a paper being submitted to some of his colleagues, and possibly to a Cabinet committee, emanating from his Ministry. I know he cannot be specific, but is there contained in it proposals for tax and other financial incentives with respect to the development of the high technology industry, particularly small business and the development of new business?
Second, does it contain, or has the Minister addressed in any way, proposals with respect to retraining of people who may be affected as a result of the development of the high technology industry that has been referred to? Does it address those two things? Third, when may we expect to see the paper tabled?

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, when I spoke of a paper I indicated earlier that I would be bringing forward a technology policy paper, which I am now doing. For some time I have had consultation and consideration in many areas. Obviously I am not at liberty to disclose to the House what is contained in that paper. I certainly will give assurance to the House that it is broad in its application in the area of technology policy in the industrial sector.
I might add that the kind of issues that the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) raises are, of course, already being addressed. The issue of fiscal incentives has been addressed. Recently some guidelines were issued to clarify some of the interpretations that have been given by the Department of National Revenue with respect to the so-called scientific research investment contracts. These matters are constantly moving forward and being reviewed. As a former Minister of National Revenue, the Hon. Member is fully aware of the activities of the interpretation section of that Department.
With respect to the issue of retraining, that is a matter which is being pursued constantly by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) through the National Training Act and other instruments. That is not to say that more should not be done. As ongoing assessments indicate to what extent technology will affect employment in these sectors, clearly action and perhaps supplemental action will have to be taken because retraining is of fundamental importance, not only to ensure that these people find jobs, but to

eliminate a certain amount of the anxiety that appears to exist in many circles with respect to the impact of technology.
Mr. Speaker, when will the paper be ready?

Mr. Speaker, one can sense an increasing awareness in this country, an awakening to the fact that we are being rapidly left behind by other more enlightened and adaptable industrialized western nations. The truth is that we are now clearly behind-left in the starting gate-in what is becoming known as the second industrial revolution, change brought on us by new technologies.
For an obvious example of how far out of the race we are, one simply has to check brand names of products sold in outlets retailing TV sets, radios, calculators, computers and other electronic gadgetry. It would be interesting to know how many Sony Walkman radios were sold this past Christmas.
After experiencing the last two years of economic turmoil in this country, many Canadians, especially those out of work, realize that something is drastically wrong. Most now sense that we must become much more than a nation whose economy is based upon the sale of its raw materials. If one examines employment statistics over past years, it can be seen that there has been a serious and growing unemployment problem in this country, long before the present recession began.
In 1966, 251,000 Canadians were out of work. By 1970, it was 476,000, by 1976, 727,000, in 1980, 867,000. Now it is in excess of 1.5 million. In fact, I heard today it is actually 1.6 million. Obviously the number of people unemployed has grown faster than the economy. Even in the good years of the sixties and seventies, unemployment was increasing and we were losing ground. A large portion of the unemployed are new entrants into the labour force, young people and an increasing number of women. I will refer to the problem of unemployment and women later.
We desperately need more jobs, not jobs of the temporary type provided by a number of Government short-term programs. 1 do not think the real and permanent-type jobs I refer to are going to come out of the resource sector. It seems logical that a good many will come out of the service sector, but the majority will have to be provided by manufacturing. This will not happen if we do not base our own economic future upon technological development. Our economy must be based upon new technologies.
Successful industrialized countries have long since realized that strong economies are based on a healthy level of research and development. This, of course, must be in tune with Government policies that create incentives for the risk-takers, a factor that is fast disappearing in this country.
We have long ago passed the period where unemployment can be solved by putting workers on the public payroll. Last year the National Research Council estimated that if Canada's 1,000 high-technology firms doubled their gross output by 1990, the net benefit to Canada's balance of payments would
amount to $12 billion and, what is so important, 650,000 jobs would be created.
The Canadian Government must, of necessity, concentrate upon working with business and labour in order to solve our economic problems. By now this Government should have realized that we are in a crisis situation. It is usual in times of crisis for all people, for all sectors, to pull together for the common good. If we hope to regain our position in the world, we must have a well-planned industrial strategy in this country. It is years and years overdue.
Industry and labour have recognized this for a good long time. Industry has also realized during this recession that, with a few exceptions, it cannot depend on Government for help. In actual fact the federal Government has appeared to be little more than an aimless spectator in the economic shake-out in the past two-years.
At a recent Toronto seminar sponsored by the Conference Board of Canada dealing with the drafting of a national industrial strategy, Mr. John Shepherd, Chairman of Leigh Instruments of Ottawa, said:
-the private sector has been too passive and defensive in front of government, waiting to react rather than hastening to contribute.
I believe that our job is to insist on a more intelligent framework, a better ordering of priorities . .. and to help bring to bear on government a better sense of the market forces which are and will be at play . . . We need to inject ourselves more forcibly and responsibility into that process.
Labour is also anxious and willing to co-operate. At the same Toronto meeting Shirley Carr, Executive Vice-President of the Canadian Labour Congress, also called for a national industrial game plan. She said:
-the creating of an atmosphere wherein shared decision-making power amongst the actors can occur is mutual recognition . . . labour has a legitimate place in Canadian society-a place that not only includes the right to organize and represent workers through collective bargaining, but also extends a seat at the table at all levels of decision-making.
One of the key elements in the Japanese success story is an industrial strategy that incorporates input from many sectors. Before any changes are made, or new initiatives taken, the Japanese Government consults with and seeks advice from representatives of industry, labour, universities and the mass media. Therefore, when a new policy affecting industry is announced, it is widely supported and is effective because of a spirit of co-operation. The Japanese strategy now has the industrial sector supporting 65 per cent of that country's research and development. Long-term, risky and expensive research is left to the Government. Recently, the Japanese Government spent $5 billion in U.S. currency in building a research centre near Tokyo which houses 40 different research groups.
I know that in this country previous and present Ministers have been canvassing representatives of industry. The previous Minister found that industry was concerned with a number of issues. Lack of start-up capital, difficulties with debt financing, a need for research and development tax incentives and a desire for more collaboration among Government, industry
February 4, 1983

and universities were subjects brought to his attention. I am sure the present Minister is going over the same ground. I hope he includes labour in his discussions. The pity is that this Government has spent too much time studying and too little time implementing, and now we are falling well behind our competitors.
My colleague, the Elon. Member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook), in a question to the Minister, quoted from a letter from Mr. Jack Donegani, the President of the Professional Institute of the Public Service of Canada, which appeared in today's Globe and Mail. I would like to quote again from that letter. The heading reads, "Stronger position urged on high-technology policy". It goes on to read:
The Professional Institute, which represents some 5,000 scientists, for years has been pressing the Government to develop and encourage research and higher technology in Canada in general, and within the federal service in particular. It has urged the Government to recognize the obvious, that advanced research and technology are imperative to the wellbeing of every Canadian, to economic development, to health, safety and security.
The institute, therefore, urges Mr. Johnston to take a stronger position in Cabinet on this issue.
We are also being warned by the Science Council of Canada that the United States and Japan are front runners in microelectronics, and Canada would be "hard-pressed to catch even the less advanced "second-tier" nations in Europe and Scandinavia". The micro-chip, a tiny silicon block which can be the equivalent of up to 500,000 transistors or more, is revolutionizing manufacturing in advanced industrialized countries. To the best of my knowledge, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Government has only dedicated about $10 million in chip research. By contrast, other countries have sensed the crisis situation which exists. France, for example, has launched a five-year, $27 billion program to ensure that she becomes a world power in computers, office equipment and consumer electronics. The $27 billion will be spent on new plants, research and development and on various subsidy programs. "Made in France" stamped on electronic gadgets will soon be as common as "Made in Japan". West Germany has a three-year $225 million program under way which grants firms up to $400,000 to promote the use of the micro-chip in their plants and products. Interestingly, applications for grants take an average of only three weeks to process. Contrast that, if you will, with the time it generally takes to get money from our federal Government for any such program. The urgency of the situation is well understood by other countries.
The micro-chip is revolutionizing the world and Canadians must realize what this means. Women, especially, are going to feel its effects. Many jobs traditionally held by women, such as in offices, as bank tellers, retail clerks and telephone operators, will be lost. In my home town of Williams Lake, British Columbia, 50 telephone operators will lose their jobs to new technology in mid-1984. Yet little, if anything, is being done to direct women from areas which will be hit hard by efficiency and productivity improvements resulting from the implementation of micro-electronic technology. Women must awake, unite and demand quick answers from Governments, industry and labour to this very urgent problem.
Supply
I suggest to the Minister and the Government that they must place the subject of technological change, and our failure to recognize the importance of research and development, on a very urgent priority basis. They must use research and development as the foundation of an industrial strategy. I suggest a conference of the federal and provincial Governments, industry, labour and representatives of our educational system should be held immediately with a view to positive direction and immediate action. We have talked for years, Mr. Speaker, about what we are going to do in this country as far as research and development and industrial strategy are concerned. Time for talk is long past. We must act. If we fail to realize the importance and urgency of the second industrial revolution, we will pay very dearly.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the remarks of the Hon. Member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist) this morning, and he placed in a very interesting context the whole question of research and development, which he also linked with tax policy and macroeconomic policy and, indeed, strategy on economic development.
After a very difficult period in the world economy, we are now seeing some indicators which are encouraging, and it is important now that the remainder of the 1980s be a period of economic renewal for us, of ensuring Canada's prosperity. Our traditional industries are the backbone of Canada and they can and should remain the source of jobs and income for thousands of Canadians. With continued productivity improvements and new marketing techniques, the traditional industries, such as fishing, forestry, mining and agriculture, can play a central role in Canada's future economic prosperity. When combined with advances in high technology sectors and the securing of Canada's industrial heartland, a positive climate of growth will re-assert itself, allowing for the necessary market adjustments to keep Canada competitive. And with growth we will have the opportunity of ensuring that every region of Canada benefits. The challenge of economic renewal calls for the co-operation of all of us, the federal and provincial Governments, unions, management, academics and consumer groups. We need to deal competently and humanely with the present and we need intelligent medium and long-term planning.
Japan provides a startling example of what is possible, and a number of speakers today have made reference to this. Poorly equipped to deal with the energy crisis, Japan has nevertheless performed very well. The key to its success has been industrial re-deployment, harnessing the most advanced technologies in order to achieve overwhelming competitive advantages. Between 1970 and 1974, while the rest of the OECD countries were worrying about short-term issues, the Japan Computer Usage Development Institute, a Government sponsored body, developed a long-term econmic strategy to make full industrial use of the then infant technology, micro-electronics. This, coupled with advanced Japanese management methods, helped propel Japan to its present industrial position.
The long awaited world economic recovery will not solve Canada's structural problems. Newly industrialized countries,

February 4, 1983
Supply
such as South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore, are using their low labour costs to achieve comparative advantages in many conventional industrial fields, such as textiles, shoes, light machinery, calculators and so on. The reindustrializing countries, such as Japan and France, are threatening both Canada's traditional industries and our high-tech sectors. Canada may have to follow the example of Japan and France and draw a blueprint for a long-term economic development plan based on micro-electronics. But the emphasis on high technology should never be interpreted to be at the expense of Canada's traditional industries. On the contrary, high technology innovation holds the potential for remarkable productivity gains in our traditional industries and, therefore, for greater job security and improved salaries for core workers.
We are blessed with natural resources and they can and should be tapped in the most profitable manner possible. We are also blessed with a competent and well educated work force. While they may have to retrain, as the Minister has just said, they are better equipped to do so than the labour force in the countries of some of our competitors. Faced with these new challenges, we need to open up the decision-making process. We need input from scientists, but we also need input from the people actually doing the job, and we must be very concerned to keep our human values. Speaking in this House on February 6, 1981, I said:
When I talk about an industrial strategy, I think of a set of policies, of an orderly and integrated way of co-ordinating government policies and, above all, of a human approach with care for the ideals of social justice, for individual dignity, for safety in the workplace and for industrial democracy. Occupational health and safety must be a particular concern at the present time, because we are still losing far more days of work and industrial productivity as a result of illness or injury on the job than as a result of strikes. Unless there is a progressive sharing of the material wealth of society, unless there is active participation in decision-making by the workers who produce that wealth, we will not succeed and, perhaps, we would not deserve to succeed.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, those principles also apply to the application of new technology. Firms facing the need to improve productivity often think first of reducing staff. Yet there is substantial evidence that industrial engineering approaches are more effective. Workers know the processes, know the plant, and if they are actively involved in decision making they can often point the way to procedures which allow the same number of people to stay at work but work in ways that yield greater profits and job satisfaction. The moneys which the federal Government has made available to labour for continued education are being well used, and are increasingly resulting in well informed and sophisticated labour leaders who have much to contribute to our future industrial development.
These people-oriented initiatives may not sound as glamorous or exciting as talk of industrial restructuring and technological innovation, but it is people who will bring forward and implement solutions. In these times we need new ideas and continual examination of the adequacy of our policies and programs.
The very rapid changes in the international economic order demand of Canada an extremely alert business intelligence system and response mechanism. The cornerstone is the free market sytem with its built-in incentives to keep pace with or ahead of international development. But one must ask, could this cornerstone be more effectively supported by Government? Public interventions are often viewed by the private sector as restrictive. Yet the private sector is frequently unable to mount effective competition in the international field without direct or indirect Government support. The success thus far achieved by the Telidon project, for example, would not have been possible without major Government participation in research and development, manufacturing seed-money and marketing. Similarly, the recent Bombardier deal in the U.S. was secured in part because of Government support in allowing for low interest loans to finance the operation.
There are, of course, significant success stories which are a credit to the Government's initiative and the entrepreneurship of the Canadian private sector, for example, Northern Telecom, Mitel, NABU, and so on. Yet the public-private interface in Canada is not carefully brought out, and golden opportunities are sometimes missed. There is, in my view, a gap in coordination between the private and public sector. However, there are several other important gaps. Federal-provincial confrontation frequently prevents co-ordinated development strategy; Canada's labour-management interface is the adversary system with too much mistrust prevailing on both sides; the University-Government interface is not so much an adversary system as a tradition of mutual indifference, in sharp contrast to the experience in European countries and Japan. A positive creative force must replace the apprehension and fear which pervades so much current economic thinking. A proactive and concerted strategy is called for, one that associates Government, labour and management and universities in a long-term planning exercise, and which distributes the fruits of innovation in such a way that as many people as possible, if not everyone, benefit. Harmonization of public and private policies, labour and management aspirations, and of federal and provincial interventions must be the wave of the future.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to approach this subject perhaps from a slightly different point of view from what we have heard. I believe the case has been made on all sides of the House that we are spending an inadequate amount of money, we have no over-all plan for research and development and, as a result, we are faced with an unemployment situation which is tragic for a great many people. My comments are directed to the parents of Canada and, I suspect, to anyone who has yet to determine what his or her eventual career will be. Even if they are pursuing a career, I would ask them seriously to consider taking a look at the broad field of science and technology, because that is where the future lies.
Diebold is perhaps one of the leading management philosophers of the world. In the 1950s he made this statement, and I see no reason to doubt it, particularly at this time, that every person would likely have seven different occupations in the
February 4, 1983

course of his lifetime. Even then Diebold could see the revolution which has been taking place.
Initially we went through the age of crafts and guilds. That led into the industrial revolution, mass production and factory jobs. Now we have another revolution upon us. We are entering the age of servo-mechanisms and the robot. I am delighted, because in the initial stages men became slaves to machines, and we now enter the new world where machines will be slaves to men. Every man must do all he can to take advantage of what is taking place. The future holds many areas of great growth that will bring hundreds of thousands of new jobs that were not even contemplated a few years ago. We do not know what the next major breakthrough will be, but we know that those who educate themselves in the sciences will be able to adapt much more easily and rapidly to what may come.
A good example is biological research. Do young people realize that we have developed enzymes that eat oil spills and that there are also enzymes that separate oil and sand? Then there is the whole area of the human condition and drugs and blood. And where are the biological breakthroughs that will change waste into useful products?
When I speak of science 1 do not mean just industrial research which makes use of what comes from pure science. Pure science is responsible for the laser, and industrialists are responsible for the literally thousands of uses that laser has been put to. Fibre optics came from pure research, as did the silicone chip. If we do not raise the amount of moneys available to universities, even without knowing what developments may result, then we must take a back seat to the rest of the world. It is from pure research and pure science that new developments come.
Young people should consider some of the following areas when thinking of careers. We have yet to develop the perfect ship. As a Member from the Pacific coast, I believe that the perfect ship is long overdue. Then there is the whole area of oceanography. The pittance that we spend on oceanography when we are surrounded on three sides by water, is ridiculous. Fish farming is another area, as is the whole area of agriculture in one form or another.
I should like to ask this and any succeeding Government of this country, where do the priorities lie? Where is their understanding of what is happening in the world? Where is Canada's George Washington Carver, the man who, in the 1920s, found over 100 uses for the peanut? Does anyone think that we would ever have had insulin if Banting and Best had had to deal with a bureaucratic structure of Government like that which exists today?
Where are the new strains of wheat? Disease-resistant wheat has been developed but little research is being done on wheat for new uses or on new crops. That is where the future of our country lies, but not sufficient work is being done in those areas.
With all due respect I would point out that the average stenographer, male or female, is as out of date as the buggy
Supply
whip salesman is today. Advertisements for help in the newspapers call for people with knowledge of computers or word processors. What a marvellous thing it would have been if this could have been foreseen five or ten years ago. Perhaps we could have arranged for this type of training in the schools a long time ago and have the people available today. Now we are attempting to catch up, but unfortunately a lot of people will be left behind.
A revolution is taking place in the office today. The word processor and the small computer are changing the nature of the individual office in the country more than the invention of the calculator or the typewriter did 50 or 60 years ago.
Where are the jobs going to be in the future? Despite the neglect by the Government and despite the fact that we are not doing what we should in terms of research, science offers the greatest future to young people.
I have no hesitation in taking another man's words when he expresses in a better form what I wish to express. In November, 1981, Dr. Larkin Kerwin of the National Research Council said:
We are a nation rich in ideas. Japan does so much with so little; we do so little with so much.
At that time he also said:
If we fail to exploit these current technological opportunities, or fail to develop new ones continually, we may still survive as woodcutters. But we must then be content with a woodcutter's wage.
The young people of this country should think about that, Mr. Speaker. They should think whether they want to be woodcutters or have a meaningful career. When I speak of science, I do not necessarily mean that one has to be a research scientist with a PhD, working in a university. 1 mean that they should take as much science as they possibly can. There will always be captains, generals, sergeants and troops, and the more training they have, the further up the ladder they will be in the new industries of the future.
Tomorrow, there could be a breakthrough that could mean that Five years from now hundreds of thousands of jobs would become available through something that we do not contemplate even in our wildest dreams at the moment. Just look at the explosion that has taken place with computers. To paraphrase a line from Time magazine, if the automobile industry had gone ahead as rapidly as the computer industry has, today you would be able to buy a Rolls-Royce for $2.40 and get 400 miles to the gallon of gasoline. IBM sends its senior computer people into the field for a year, then they must go back to school. They go back to the field for another year, and back to school again. The company believes that if senior computer people are left in the field for two years, they will not be familiar with the technology that is being developed.
At the present time Canada spends less on real research than any other industrialized country, says Larkin Kerwin. Not all the National Research Council's projects under the Industrial Research Assistance Program were sure-fire winners. The average was $20 in sales for every dollar of NRC R and D funding. But 80 per cent of the projects have led to

February 4, 1983
Supply
direct or indirect benefits. Just under half of them produced $1.8 billion in sales, 16 per cent are confidently expected to produce sales in the future, while 24 per cent gave indirect benefits. When a research body can produce as many jobs and as much wealth for the country as that, then it is very, very foolish for a government to starve it to death as this Government has been doing for years. If the Liberal Government had put that kind of emphasis on research and development when it came in with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1968, I doubt if there would be any unemployment in the country today.
We just have to look at what Japan has done in terms of research and development and see how it has affected their standard of living. Their economy is far ahead of ours.
In 1968 we spent 1.4 per cent of the Gross National Product in the vital area of research; today we spend only 1.13 per cent, which is up 0.9 per cent from two years ago. Fifteen years after 1968, the Government has moved the target back up to 1.5 per cent for 1985. To reach this modest target, R and D spending must not only outstrip inflation, it must increase in real terms by 18 per cent per year. These are staggering figures. But as a percentage of population Canada had one-third as many people working in research and development as did the Swedes, the Germans or the Japanese. We had one-half as many as the Dutch, the French and the Americans. We spend less per capita on research and development than all industrialized nations, with the exceptions of Ireland and Iceland. That is a record of which we should all be thoroughly ashamed. In fact, if we raise our percentage of GNP expended on R and D by just one percentage point, we could ultimately provide one million new jobs in this country and generate those $20 billion in new manufacturing sales.
I believe that requires some dramatic tax reforms regarding investments in high technology. If this country can afford to give total write-offs on third-rate motion pictures, we can certainly do no less for high-tech investment which will ensure a viable future for our children. To me it is deplorable that this country and this Government do not realize what the pay-offs are in research. This Government brags about this scheme or that scheme. Some are excellent, and for this they ought to be complimented. But we have a philosophical base here which is dead wrong, in my view. That philosophical base is grants, which means the Ottawa bureaucrats decide which company goes ahead and which company does not. Bureaucrats are not good businessmen. As a Conservative, 1 believe that what should be done is to have a system of incentives. What we should do is to say, "There is the incentive. Go after it, fellow. If you make it, great. If you are inefficient and you cannot do it, down the drain you go." But incentives for research and development should be given to all through the tax system. We should not have bureaucrats trying to run the whole show. We have seen the disastrous results and the wasted taxpayers's dollars when bureaucrats have made terrible errors in judgment.
In conclusion, I want to quote from what Mr. Walter F. Light said. He is the President and Chief Executive Officer of Northern Telecom Limited. Last April he said:
R and D, like capital spending in plant and equipment, is not an expense, it is an investment in the future. High technology companies must constantly innovate to maintain their leadership and ability to compete.
The commitment to research and development must be consistent and long term. In the long run, the winners will be those companies that maintain R and D investment in every economic climate and, when their profits are rising, recognize this as an opportunity to step up their R and D spending to an even higher level.
To compete, a company, an industry, or a country, must pursue a clear strategy, focusing its efforts and resources on the areas of greatest opportunity. It must maintain a consistent and growing commitment to research and development. It must invest in the development of people in schools, in universities, and in business. It must move quickly and decisively to respond to market opportunities.
Mark Twain made a statement on the weather. Everybody talks about it but nobody does anything about it. The weather is another major area for research. But I think we have talked enough about research and development. It is almost like motherhood. I have yet to hear Government Members say that they are not in favour of it, but I have yet to see a fully meaningful policy from the Government on research, and the Government should have one. We can go right back to 1970 and the Senate report. Nothing has happened. Let me say to the Government of Canada, for the sake of the youth of this country, for the sake of the unemployed, for the standard of living for our children, get on with it and let us get the money going in research in the amounts that are needed.

speakeroldname: Mr. AI MacBain (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think we all appreciate the motion put forward for discussion today by the Hon. Member for Scarborough East (Mr. Gilchrist). It is a timely topic and it is one we must address. I enjoyed the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Scarborough East. I also enjoyed hearing from the Hon. Member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) who has just addressed the House, as well as many others.
I want to mention a very small program of the Government of Canada and pay tribute to it. It is one of the smallest in the area of research and development. However, there has been some discussion as to whether or not it will be continued. I hope it will. The program is known as the New Crop Development Fund. I believe the total amount committed to that program is only three-quarters of a million dollars. Speaking only for my area with regard to this fund and the research and development permitted under it, the farmers and those producers of goods in the agricultural sector appreciate this program very much.
I noticed in a booklet entitled "The Government of Canada's Investment in Science" a very interesting opening remark. It reads:
Research and development (R and D) and industrial innovation are key elements in the federal government's policies and strategies to meet the economic challenges of the future.
I read that because I like the connection between research and development and industrial innovation. I think that is a
February 4, 1983

very important point and it is a linkage that is very often missed. There is a danger, as was found in the United States, that when a tremendous amount of money is put into research and development, the next step, commercialization, does not happen. It does not happen because sometimes we fail to appreciate and make possible the movement from R and D to commercialization. It is one thing to permit, in one way or another, the funds for R and D to be made available, but after the research and development is done, before the product or the technology is on the commercial market, a big gap occurs. The authorities in the United States feel that it takes eight years to move an innovative venture, that is, the product or the technology, from the completion of research and development to profitable commercialization. Those same authorities state that it takes 12 years for a company in a normal or average case to make the same return on investment from an innovative new venture, when you compare that venture with a mature one.
When you look at a period of eight years before a product becomes profitable and a 12 year period before it brings a return on your investment, Mr. Speaker, you realize the importance of the time frame. Small companies cannot overcome this obstacle. I say to the Hon. Member for Scarborough East that, as well as having a research and development policy or strategy, we must also take a look at the next step, that is, what happens between the time when R and D is carried out and the time when a company makes a return on the investment on the product or technology.
I am aware of the fact that the statistics I have just quoted are American, but I think they are so basic that they cannot be much different in Canada, that is to say, that it takes eight years to start turning a profit in the average case taken from a study of 68 industries involved in the innovative ventures, and 12 years to return the investment.
When we, as Members of Parliament, are considering research and development, we must realize that there is an important linkage between R and D and the commercialization of a product. Unless research and development is given assistance to make such projects profitable, it is unlikely that the millions and billions of dollars to be poured into research and development will be of any great benefit.
1 personally believe that in order to have a meaningful research and development program, there must be a national industrial strategy in place. I appreciate the fact that the Hon. Member for Scarborough East was not attempting to put one ahead of the other, but I suggest that we need a comprehensive and long-term industrial strategy for Canada, part of which would be a research and development policy. I think this is extremely important.
I had the opportunity to present a submission on an industrial strategy for Canada before the Macdonald Commission. I suggested that the Commission make a preliminary report to the Government of Canada asking it not to wait for the economic report from the Macdonald Commission but to set
Supply
up a group consisting of businessmen, labour leaders, university people and members from the federal and provincial Governments to prepare an industrial strategy for Canada. This group should also receive information about the state of affairs outside of Canada since 30 per cent of our industrial output is exported.
As I pointed out in my letter to the Macdonald Commission, I do not believe that an industrial strategy for Canada can be prepared within the House of Commons, regardless of which Party is in power, if we depend upon the resources available to a government or its Departments. I say this because Ministers of the Crown and their senior advisers already have a very heavy daily administrative burden. I am sure all Members agree that backbenchers are very busy, and surely Ministers are extremely busy running their Departments. We should not wait for an industrial strategy to be developed in the House because it will not happen.
An industrial strategy is essential for the future well-being of this country. This industrial strategy should be developed outside of the House. There are retired businessmen, retired labour leaders, university people and bankers as well as consulting firms who have a great knowledge to contribute in the formation of an industrial strategy. A strong team must be formed that can give us a comprehensive industrial strategy, which will include a system for research and development and the commercialization of the fruits of that research and development as one of its goals.
1 pointed out to the Commission that during wartime we adopted a dollar a year idea. I think that we are in position where the economy of this country and the western world is such that we could adopt a warlike innovative action which would be justifiable and acceptable if it resulted in an industrial strategy for Canada. I have learned from major industrial concerns that this is their position. They are prepared to make their top company personnel available to contribute to this industrial strategy since it is their belief that it would be very good for the bottom line of their companies to have a longterm industrial strategy for Canada. However, they would not consider this if it is not connected to the bottom line of their financial sheet.
As I said, I have asked the Macdonald Commission to make a preliminary report such as I have suggested. If that report is delivered, I believe Members would support the Government in setting up a group to form a comprehensive industrial strategy. While it would be best to wait for a report from the Macdonald Commission on an industrial strategy, I do not believe that we can afford the luxury of waiting for it. 1 might say that this is also the opinion of industrial leaders whom I have consulted.
It is not uncommon to hear after-dinner speakers tell their audiences that the day of the smokestack industry in Canada is gone. They will go on to say that the day of the textile industry in Canada is gone, the shoe industry has disappeared, and some go as far as to say-if not publicly, certainly in private conversation-that the automobile industry will either be unimportant or a thing of the past. These remarks are made by

February 4, 1983
Supply
some very important people in governments, industry and education. Responsible people have tried to justify these statements on the basis that a third wave of high-tech industries will employ young Canadians and remove the need for those industries which I have mentioned. When this is said without any in depth study or industrial strategy to back it up, it may result in our having to pay a heavy price in the future for those remarks.
A Member from the New Democratic Party said earlier this morning that there is no concrete evidence available that third wave industries will be of such great strength or have such a large number of employees that they will take the place of the older industries that have been part of the industrial revolution in Canada. I agree with that statement. 1 am sorry that he is not in the House this afternoon, but I am sure that he will read it in Hansard. What 1 am saying is that when we make statements like that, when speaking to our constituents or in the House, before we know what we are talking about and before we know what the future holds, we are doing a disservice to this country. That is not to say that the third wave industries will not be helpful and beneficial to this country and a boon to our young people. However, I am saying that 1 have no evidence that one type of industry will be a complete substitute for the other. If we move in that direction without knowing what we are really doing, we will in all likelihood lay a false foundation for the industrial future of this country, and I, for one, will not participate in the movement in this direction.
I hope that when the opportunity arises, Hon. Members from all sides will support the idea of an out-House industrial strategy being prepared for Canada, because I do not think we will see it unless it is done that way. It can be done under the direction of the Government of the day, the Government of which I am honoured to be a Member at this time. However, it must be very broadly based, along the lines that I suggested. That does not mean that Government Ministers, Deputy Ministers and senior experts in various fields cannot be assigned to this group to ensure that part of the expertise found in the elected or appointed people in Government is fully utilized. They do have a real contribution to make. Ministers have a great deal to offer in the experience they have gained in running large Departments. This is true of Deputy Ministers and various experts in the Departments as well.
As I see it, however, the real expertise for an industrial strategy in Canada must come from those in the private sector to a very large extent. They are the ones who know how to run the country, not Government Ministers, Deputy Ministers or experts in a tiny field in a Department who are qualified to advise a Minister or Deputy Minister on a small issue. When it comes to an issue involving an industrial strategy for Canada well into the twenty-first century, it requires the expertise which we do not have here.
Speaking before the Macdonald Commission, I stated my opinion that not all expertise may be found in Canada itself. We depend on the international market for our sales, and there would be nothing wrong if some of the people we retained to help this group came from some of the countries that take large amounts of our exports.

I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls for his very serious presentation. I hope he will not mind if I just give him one little jibe over his terminology. I was not too sure what he meant by an "out-House industrial policy". I sort of thought that that is perhaps what we already had. Seriously, I did want to ask him about his concern over the strategy of the Government not embracing the textile or the shoe, or the other "low technology" industries, although it is not really fair to call them "low technology". I remind him that the Minister stated that "it is in these high technologyintensive sectors, and I believe in these sectors alone, that new challenging and high-paying jobs can be created". I am wondering if the Hon. Member for Niagara Falls does not support that view. Will he attempt to convince the Minister that perhaps in areas other than the advancing technologies we should be supporting business?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question. I would like to mention that I think I deserve the jibe that the Hon. Member has given me. Being a farmer's son, I should have been more careful. The phrase "in-House" is now such a part of my vocabulary that I forgot about my past, and 1 should never do that.
I would say that my view is not necessarily ad idem with the statement of the Minister which the Hon. Member for Scarborough East has quoted. I am trying to be fair. I know there is a place in Canada for high-tech. It is obvious. However, 1 am afraid that in our rush to get the high-tech, we are forgetting about the bread and butter industries of the past, and that is what I am against. It may be that when a comprehensive industrial strategy is prepared in the manner I have suggested to the House this afternoon, I will be proven wrong, and that we could move in the direction as stated by the Minister of the Government. However, 1 am certainly not prepared to accept that statement at this time without the in-depth study which I see as being required. I hope that this answer is helpful.

I would like to make a comment and direct a question to the Hon. Member whose speech I very much enjoyed. I liked his use of the term "out-House strategy". It opens up lots of possibilities. We could have Eaton's to catalogue it, for example, we could have the former Alberta Cabinet Minister, Mr. Horst Schmid, to testify about it, and so on. The possibilities are simply endless. My colleagues also have some comments, but they are probably not permitted in Hansard.
The term "industrial strategy" is not a new one. The present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), has used the term, as did his great friend, John Turner, when he was Minister of Finance.

February 4, 1983

As Don McGillivray, the journalist, said last week, "all God's children" have used the term "industrial strategy".
All Ministers of Industry, for sure.

But what does it really mean? 1 would like to direct two questions to the Parliamentary Secretary, who I think is one of the most thoughtful Members of this House. I might say that I agree with what he has said about moving too quickly in high-tech without thinking about it. I think he is right-on there. However, has the Parliamentary Secretary given any thought to the use of another term for industrial strategy, something else we could call it which would better reflect the process? Second, how does he see labour's involvement in the process? He spoke of business being a big part of the industrial strategy. How does he view labour's participation in the new industrial age or in the process of forming an industrial strategy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not attempt to explain what I envisage an industrial strategy as being, because if I went into that subject, I think it would take away from what I expect the group to do, because even defining it will not be easy. I was using the term today in the way it is normally used.
I am interested in the Hon. Member's question as it pertains to labour. I was speaking without notes and I meant to say "labour, business, university personnel and others". I will check the "blues", and it may be that I did not make that point as strongly as 1 had intended. If I did not do so, I do so now. I point out that on Tuesday of this week, I appeared on a TV show with Mr. Cliff Pilkie of the Ontario Federation of Labour. We discussed this very point. We were in agreement on the basic idea of an industrial strategy somewhat along the lines I have suggested today. Certainly the idea was put forward that labour would play a very important part in the preparation of that strategy. This is not to say that Mr. Pilkie did not say there would be difficulties in getting the three together in an industrial strategy for Canada. There was no suggestion at all that it would not work. It was my first opportunity to meet Mr. Pilkie, which probably explains why I may not be as close to labour as I should be. In any event, I enjoyed meeting him. After the show was over, my guess was that labour was just as interested as business and Government in getting together to lay down a foundation for the future economic development of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to participate in the debate precipitated by the motion which in part reads:
That this House recognizes that an increased commitment to science and technology is fundamental to the establishment of a new industrial base in Canada, to the rejuvenation of existing industries, to the creation of new employment and the maintenance of existing jobs, and to economic recovery-
Perhaps some of the most important inadequacies of the Liberal Government, which we can understand best in terms of current economic conditions, were described in the December issue of "Economic Outlook". It gave the figures which OECD provided, comparing Canada with the other OECD countries.
Supply
Three parameters were used which I think provided us with a context with which to compare Canada and the other nations in terms of how we were really doing. The first parameter was ranking in terms of economic growth. Canada ranked twenty-fourth out of 24. I could go through the list. It included Australia, Austria, Belgium, Turkey, Portugal, Luxembourg, etc.
The second parameter was that in the top seven OECD countries we had the second worst record in unemployment levels. Again this provided us with a comparison to use. The problems that we face in the area of research and development stem from five basic areas. First, we have to be funding a much higher level of basic research in this country. Talking about applied research and the adaptation of existing technology is certainly of importance. However, any country that is going to advance technologically, that is going to stay at the forefront and compete effectively with other nations in this world in the new technologies and the technologies of the future will have to be concerned with funding a substantial body of basic and fundamental research.

Fourth, and this is where we start to get into the area of industrial strategy, and I have great difficulty with the notions sometimes put forward about an industrial strategy that calls on Governments to direct. Canada has serious difficulties in all of these areas. In my opinion we are under-funding basic research. We are not utilizing our existing body of research talent, whether it be at the National Research Council, in the universities, the colleges or the private research foundations. They are being underfunded. They are not being provided with the kinds of funds necessary for release time so as to allow them to do increased amounts of research, and as a result we are under-utilizing the talents available to us now. We do not have an advanced program of aid for young people to promote excellence, to promote a science "meritocracy", if you will, and that has to be improved greatly. We do not have the kind of management training which is required to ensure that our scientists have available to them those who are able to put the process in an effective format.

Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few words and to commend Members for the very positive debate we have had. I would like to commend the mover of the motion who placed it on the Order Paper. Since I have only about four or five minutes, I want to come directly to the point and suggest that what this House should be doing is to establish a committee of the House to study the social and economic impact of technological change. That might be a way to bring some fruition to all of the ideas that we have spoken about today. As legislators we might have some input into what kind of society and vision we have for this country. I think we all recognize that advanced technology is here. We are experiencing some tremendous technological restructuring throughout the world. We cannot turn back the clock. We cannot close our eyes to what is happening. It is here and it is happening now and it will continue in the future.
Really what we have to do is to ask ourselves a couple of questions. At what pace do we want to have that change brought into Canada? On what kind of industries do we want to concentrate? How will it affect human beings? Will we have a society in the future making these machines and computers to be the slaves of mankind, as someone said, rather than human beings becoming the slaves of the computer? Will we have the kind of society where we control the robots, or will the robots control us? For those kinds of reasons I think it is important that we go to all three House leaders and ask for a committee of this House to be set up to look into the social and economic impact of technological change.
When I look around the world I see a tremendous revolution taking place. There is a tremendous recession in the world. Part of the reason for that recession is to be found in the result of technological change. I am not sure whether any country or political Party has found the solution to which way we should be going. Certainly no political Party has found all the solutions. We have had many different attempts. We find, for example, that the more mature industries that we have known in the past, such as steel, auto, rubber and glass, will not be the industries of the future in terms of providing many jobs and many workers. Even if we have a world running at full capacity and we are over the recession, technological change will make it so that these industries will never employ the number

of people they employed in the past. I am not saying that these industries are obsolete. 1 am saying that while the technologies we knew in the past are obsolete, the industries are not obsolete. We will have to keep many of these more mature industries, but we will have to make sure that we have the most modern technology so that they do not disappear, that they are internationally competitive and we can export around the world as well as supply our own market.
On September 25, I had the chance to speak in Chicago to a convention of the United Auto Workers of America. Those people are most concerned about the unemployed in their industry. From their studies they told me that by the year 2000 even if the Americans regain their full share of the auto industry, from the Japanese and the Europeans, about 80 per cent of the jobs they knew in 1980 will have disappeared because of advanced technology, the robots and the fully automated factories. The Japanese now have factories that are 98 per cent robotized. These are questions that we will have to look at as Parliamentarians. We will have to find solutions to these questions. If we do not, we will have more and more people unemployed, disillusioned and turned off by this failure of leadership in the country. That is why 1 argue very strongly that a committee be set up.
About two weeks ago, an American economist named Thurow appeared before a policy convention of the Liberal Party of Ontario. He said that what we lack in this country is a vision or a dream of where we are going as a society. We do not have that economic strategy or policy. He said that the Austrians have an objective, even though that country is situated right next door to such a powerful country as Germany. The Austrians' objective is to be better and richer than the Germans. The Austrians have met that challenge. They have succeeded. I think we in this country can learn from
countries such as Austria, Scandinavia, France, West Germany and Japan.
In closing I urge Members of all three Parties in this House to approach their House leaders and try to get a committee going very soon, because we are lagging behind in this country in the field of advanced technology.

Mr. Speaker, if I may interject, I am intrigued by the thought of a special committee of the House of Commons, the idea of setting up a kind of task force which was put forward by the Hon. Member for York-ton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom). Would the hon. gentleman be in favour, as well as establishing such a task force, of restructuring the Standing Committees of the House of Commons so that a standing committee of the House of Commons might be struck to deal with matters on an ongoing basis beyond the task force, having regard to the fact that we have come to the day when we must specialize in our committee structure?

The simple answer to that is yes. I think the Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) is absolutely right. I would support any move in that direction and I would appeal to all Members of the House to support that suggestion also.
